div.p: Schedulability analysis is very important for hard realtime systems. Classical analysis techniques of fixed priority scheduling do not integrate system overheads into the feasibility condition, so these theories and methods can not directly be applied in practical environments. This paper presents a method to compute the worst-case response time of non-preemptable periodic tasks in an OSEK compliant system, and then establishes the feasibility condition. The proposed method takes into account the identified main overheads of a typical OSEK system, and integrates these into classic analysis techniques. Experiment results show that the method is applicable and effective, and can be used in real-time system designs with an OSEK system.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Hard real-time constraints are pervasive in control systems nowadays, such as traction control, anti-lock break systems and engine control in a typical vehicle control system. Hard real-time means that a task must fulfill execution strictly before its absolute deadline, otherwise there will be severe consequences. It can be formulated as follows: any task τ i released at time t, must finish its execution before time t + D i , where D i and t + D i are called the relative and absolute deadline of task τ i , respectively. In such a system, it should be proven that all tasks must meet their deadline requirements before the costly implementation phase. Although simulation method can be used to verify the hard real-time constraint, this method suffers from several fallacies such as time inefficiency and insufficiency in strictly proving the schedulability of the system.

Scheduling theory [9], as it applies to hard real-time environment, has been extensively studied in the past several decades. Fixed priority scheduling, which is easy to imple-ment and requires relatively low system overheads, is very common in embedded operating systems, such as the OSEK operating system. There have been some full-fledged analysis techniques [8,6,5,10] to solve fixed priority scheduling problem, but these techniques are not directly suitable for an OSEK [3] compliant system, because the scheduling policy of the OSEK OS is more complicated, and for practical reasons we should take kernel overheads of the real time operating system into account [2]. In this paper, we will propose a method to analyze the fixed priority non-preemptive scheduling in the OSEK operating system. Thus it is possible to prove an OSEK application system schedulable at design time before implementation. This paper is organized as follows: in section 2, the fundamentals of OSEK operating system related to our topic are introduced and then we identify the main overheads when non-preemptive scheduling policy is assumed; in section 3, we formulate the problem and compute the worstcase responding time (WCRT) to establish the feasibility condition; in section 4, experiment results are shown; and then we conclude.

div.head: OSEK OS Overview
div.p: OSEK/VDX is a joint project in the automotive industry. It aims at establishing an industry standard for an openended architecture for distributed control units in vehicles. OSEK Operating System (OSEK OS) [3] is a single processor operating system for distributed embedded control units. And it is not only suitable for an automotive control system, but also a good choice for many hard real-time applications, as it supports efficient utilization of resources and also hard real-time constraints.

div.head: OSEK Task Concepts
div.p: In an OSEK operating system [3], all tasks are statically defined at the compilation time of the whole system. OSEK operating system provides two different task models: basic task and extended task. The latter is distinguished to the former by being allowed to use the system call Wait-Event which may turn the current task into W ait state. In our analysis we only consider independent periodic tasks, between which there are no cooperations and synchronizations, thus we don't take extended task into account.

In the life time of a basic task, it changes its state between Ready, Running and Suspended. As the microprocessor can only handle one task at a time, there may be several tasks in Ready state waiting for the releasing of the CPU. Figure 1

div.head: Figure 1. Basic Task State Transition
div.p: The details of all the transitions defined in the OSEK OS standard are paraphrased as follows:
• activate: A new task is put into the Ready state which is eligible to run.
• start: A Ready task is selected to run.
• preempt: If the task is preemptable and there is a higher priority task ready to run, the current running task is preempted to yield the CPU, and put into the Ready state.
• terminate: The task completes and changes to Suspended state.
In an OSEK system every task must call TerminateTask or ChainTask (of no use for periodic tasks) to complete itself, otherwise it will result in an undefined behavior.

It should be pointed out that the OSEK operating system allows to activate a task multiple times, and this feature is key to support tasks with arbitrary deadlines. And the OSEK system also provide alarm mechanism to support periodic tasks which are common in typical control systems.

div.head: Non-Preemptive Scheduling
div.p: The OSEK operating system provides four different scheduling policies: full-preemptive, non-preemptive, groups of tasks and mixed preemptive, and we will only discuss non-preemptive scheduling here.

With the non-preemptive scheduling policy, task switching is only performed via one of a selection of explicitly defined system services (explicit points of rescheduling). The points of rescheduling for basic tasks are defined as follows:
• Successful termination of a task(system service Termi-nateTask).
• Successful termination of a task with explicit activation of a successor task(system service ChainTask).
• Explicit call of the scheduler(system service Schedule).
As aforementioned reasons, all tasks are independent in our analysis, so the only rescheduling point under consideration is the first one.

div.head: OSEK Overheads
div.p: When the fixed priority non-preemptive scheduling policy is assumed, based on the discussions of above subsections, we can identify that, for independent basic tasks, the main system overheads of the OSEK system are Activate-Task, TerminateTask and the scheduling cost of selecting the highest priority ready task to run. Note that these three kinds of overheads may be related to the number of tasks in an OSEK system, which is implementation specific.

div.head: Problem Statement
div.p: We now investigate the problem of scheduling a set Γ={τ 1 , ...τ n } of n tasks with OSEK OS overheads. Our analysis will be based on the following two assumptions about the tasks:
• Every task is periodic, and the period T i can be greater than the relative deadline D i .

• Tasks are independent to each other, and there are no precedence relations among all tasks. The precedence constraint placed by many real-time systems can be easily removed by partitioning tasks into sub-tasks or properly assigning the priorities of tasks.

A task set is said to be schedulable if and only if all the tasks in the set finish before their respective deadlines. So the key of schedulability analysis is to compute the worstcase response time of each task.
The notations in our discussion are given by Table 1.

div.head: Classical Concepts and Techniques
div.p: Before analysis, we now recall some classical concepts and techniques which are employed in our analysis.
• A task is said to be non-concrete if the first releasing time is not known a priori. In this paper we will only consider non-concrete tasks that are more general and more realistic in our problem.
• Time is assumed to be discrete, for the reason that the basic time unit in a control system is the clock cycle.

In [1], it is shown that there is no loss of generality with respect to feasibility results by restricting the schedules to be discrete, once the task parameters are assumed to be integers (multiple of the clock tick) i.e a discrete schedule exists if and only if a continuous schedule exists.

• The concept of level-i busy period [6], first proposed by Lehoczky, is a powerful tool which can support the schedulability analysis of arbitrary deadline tasks with fixed priorities. A level-i busy period is a time interval [a, b], within which tasks of priority i or higher are processed throughout [a,b] but no tasks of level i or higher are processed in (a-ε,a) or (b, b+ε) for sufficiently small ε > 0.

• All response times of the instances of task τ i are a part of some level-i busy period, thus we need only identify the phasing of τ 1 , ..., τ n which creates the longest worst-case response time of task τ i .

div.head: Related Works
div.p: The work of W. Lei, et. al. [7] gives an investigation of the overheads of OSEK operating system and suggests how to integrate these factors into analysis.
L. George, et. al. [4] assume level-i busy period analysis method to compute the worst-case response time R i of nonpreemptive scheduling, given as:

div.p: where L i is the longest level-i busy period, and w i (q) is the start time of the q th instance of task τ i . The work of F. Bimbard and L. George [2] presents a solution to feasibility condition of fixed priority preemptive scheduling integrated OSEK system overheads.

div.head: Worst-case Analysis
div.p: Our schedulability analysis is based on the computation of the worst-case response time of each task τ i . If the worstcase response time of a task is no more than its deadline, then the task is schedulable. If all the tasks in a system are schedulable, then the system is schedulable. We will use the level-i busy period analysis method to compute the worst-case response time, and then establish the feasibility condition.
As in the non-preemptive scheduling without system overheads, we should consider the blocking time from lower priority tasks.

div.head: Lemma 1
div.p: The maximum blocking time of a task τ i , denoted by B i , is given by:
div.formula: B i = max ∀j,Pj <Pi (C j + C term )(1)
div.p: Proof: A task with a lower priority than P i arriving after the critical instant 0 can not be executed in the level-i busy period. Task τ i may be blocked by only one lower priority task. In the worst case, this task would have started executing just prior to the critical instant. So the maximum blocking time for task τ i is given in equation ( 1), and we count the ending cost of this task into B i for convenience.
Lemma 2 The longest level-i busy period L i is given as:
div.formula: L i = B i + ∀j,Pj ≥Pi L i T j (C act + C sched + C j + C term ) + ∀j,Pj <Pi 1 + L i T j • C act (2)
div.p: Proof: The longest level-i busy period starts from the first critical instant 0 when task τ i and all higher priority tasks are released, and the lower priority task with the longest execution time is released just prior to time 0. So, the L i is composed of three parts:
The first part denotes the blocking time.

All the requested instances of task τ i and higher priority tasks will be finished in L i . Every task instance will be activated, scheduled to run at some time, executed and then terminated, so the second part denotes the execution time and system overheads of these tasks in the level-i busy period.
The last part denotes the activation cost of the lower priority tasks, all of which won't be executed in L i .

div.head: Lemma 3
div.p: The finish time of q th instance of task τ i in the longest level-i busy period is:
div.formula: F i (q) = B i + q • (C sched + C i + C term ) + ∀j,Pj >Pi 1 + F i (q) -C i -C term T j • (C sched + C i C term ) + ∀j 1 + F i (q) T j • C act(3)
div.p: Proof: As non-preemptive scheduling is assumed, we can infer that the q th instance of task τ i will be executed at the end of F i (q), and up to the time F i (q), q instances of task τ i and the instances of higher priority tasks released before time F i (q) -C i -C term are finished. A simple explanation of all the parts of the equation ( 3) is given as follows:
The meaning of the first part is the same as in equation (2).

The second part q • (C sched + C i + C term ) is the execution time and the system overheads of q instances of τ i . Note that we don't count the activation cost of τ i in this part, because the activation times of task τ i might be greater than q until time F i (q).

The third term is the interference from the higher priority tasks. We only need to consider the instances of these tasks arriving up to time: F i (q) -C i -C term , when the q th instance of τ i starts executing.
The last part denotes all the activation cost in the time interval [0, F i (q)].
Theorem 1 The feasibility condition of non-preemptive scheduling with OSEK system overheads is:
div.formula: U ≤ 1 (4a) ∀τ i ∈ Γ : R i ≤ D i (4b)
div.p: where
div.formula: U = ∀j C act + C sched + C j + C term T j R i = max ∀q:1≤q≤Q (F i (q) -q • T i ) Q = 1 + L i /T i
div.p: Proof: Inequality (4a) is straightforward, because the processor utilization can not be greater than 1. And this inequality should be met to guarantee the convergence of iterative computation of L i and F i (q). In [2], it is shown that the worst-case response time of a periodic task with kernel overheads is found in the longest level-i busy period, so clearly R i denotes the worst-case response time of τ i . The task set is schedulable if and only if every task's worst-case response time is not greater than its relative deadline, which is given in inequality (4b).

In summary, to test the schedulability of an OSEK system when non-preemptive scheduling policy is assumed, we must first ensure the correctness of inequality (4a), then iteratively compute the L i and F i (q) using equation ( 2) and (3) respectively, and finally check if the inequality (4b) is met.

div.head: Experiment Results
div.p: In order to verify our analysis results, we do simulation on three task sets, and then make a comparison between simulation results and our theoretical results. The key of our analysis is the computation of the worst-case response time of each task, so we only need to compare the theoretical WCRT with the simulation counterpart.

A event-driven simulation program is developed to simulate the execution sequences of a task set, with the first releasing time of every task randomly selected, and the simulation starts from time 0 and proceeds until time 600000000. After running the simulation multiple times, we can obtain the worst-case response time of each task in the set.
At the same time, a program is written to compute the theoretical WCRT according to the equations given in subsection 3.4.
The properties of the three task sets are given in Table 2.
In table 3, 4 and 5, R S i and R T i denote simulation WCRT and theoretical WCRT, respectively.
We can see from the results that, R T i is a very tight upper bound of R S i , and when CPU load is heavier, there is no penalty on the accuracy of the theoretical results.

div.head: Conclusion and Future Work
div.p: In this paper we investigate the main overheads in an OSEK operating system when non-preemptive scheduling policy is assumed, and integrate all these factors into classical schedulability analysis to establish a feasibility condition. Our experiment results show that this method is applicable and efficient.

The mixed preemptive scheduling and groups of tasks scheduling in OSEK operating system are much more complicated, because the rescheduling points of these two scheduling policies rely on the preemption property of the running task. It is not easy to estimate the preemption costs tightly, and more investigations should be done to tackle these two problems.
